title: The metta sutta, alone
tomorrow: if every blessing is "the highest," which one comes first?

lines: ONE FACE ON THE LOCK SCREEN.
A MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD.
HOW CAN EVERYONE BE THE ONE?
cards: A parent's lock screen is usually one face, maybe two. Nobody sets it to all the children in the world. That's what makes today's text strange.

The metta sutta, the Buddha's short discourse on goodwill, builds to one picture: a mother guarding her only child, with her own life if she has to. Then it asks for that same love toward every living being.
Here's the puzzle. An only child is, by definition, the one. How can everyone be your only one?

teach.b: Start where the sutta starts. Not with a feeling, with a person: someone able and upright, gentle in speech, not proud, content, living lightly, who wouldn't do even a small thing the wise would blame.
Then the wish: may all beings be happy and safe. And it won't let you leave anyone out.

teach.h: NO ONE LEFT OUT, SEEN OR UNSEEN.
teach.b: Weak or strong, long or short, big or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or still to be born. Let no one deceive another, or despise anyone anywhere. Then the mother.
Here's the solve: the picture isn't about how many. It's about how. A mother with her only child doesn't love politely.
She's watchful, wholehearted, and she'd step in front of danger. The sutta keeps that quality and removes the edge: toward all beings, a heart without limit, above, below and all around.
Then it says when: standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as you're awake. That's why Buddhists chant these verses and practice metta as a daily discipline.
And tradition tells a story with it: monks frightened in a forest were sent back with these words, and the forest turned friendly. Metta isn't a mood you wait for.
It's practiced, like a mother's attention, until it's how you look at people.

how: In Theravada communities the Karaniya Metta Sutta is chanted by monks and lay people, often at blessings and at the start of meditation, and metta practice, wishing beings well in widening circles, is taught as a daily discipline.

o: the Buddha's discourse on goodwill, a mother's care at its heart
a sutta about a mother who became a nun and a teacher
a chant that asks the Buddha for a loving family

games.q: inside the metta sutta — tap the pairs.
p: guards her only child with her life
weak or strong, seen or unseen
frightened, then sent back with it

s: metta means being nice so nobody gets upset
the sutta's picture is a mother who'd guard her child with her life: fierce care, not keeping the peace.
the sutta wishes well even to beings unseen and not yet born
seen or unseen, near or far, born or still to be born: no one is left out.
the sutta starts with the feeling of love and nothing else
it starts with a person: upright, gentle in speech, not proud, content, living lightly.

games.q: a classmate you find exhausting is sitting alone at lunch, the day after her dog died. what does the metta sutta's mother picture point to?
o: that guarding care isn't only for people you like: go sit with her
metta is a wish you hold inside; no need to change where you sit
keep your distance: goodwill for all can't mean closeness to all
games.why: the sutta asks for a mother's care toward all beings, and says when: standing, walking, sitting, as long as you're awake. it's meant to be lived, not only wished.

practice: Bring to mind one person you would guard with your life, and let that care fill your chest. Keeping it, widen it one step at a time: someone you barely know, someone hard to be around, then every being, seen and unseen.
If you like, say it under your breath: may all beings be happy.

wordCard.voice: The metta sutta: the Buddha's short discourse on goodwill, with a mother guarding her only child at its heart.

orig.note: Pali: goodwill, friendliness; the heart the sutta asks to grow without limit.

carryVoice: Keep this one: as a mother, that same care with the edge taken off. See you tomorrow.
